section.title: The Fall of Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: After a year and a half of siege, the wall is finally breached and everything Jeremiah warned for forty years arrives at once: Zedekiah captured and blinded, the city and temple burned, the people carried to Babylon. In the same chapter that records this devastation, God singles out two men for preservation, Jeremiah himself and Ebed-melech the Cushite, both spared for the same simple reason, they trusted the LORD.
section.thesis: Everything Jeremiah warned for decades arrives in a single terrible chapter, Zedekiah captured and blinded, the city burned, the people exiled, yet in the very moment of judgment God singles out for life the one prophet who spoke His word and the one foreigner who trusted Him.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the siege ends and Zedekiah's judgment is pronounced at Riblah; Jerusalem is burned and its walls broken down, with only the poorest left in the land; and Jeremiah is cared for while Ebed-melech receives a personal promise of deliverance because he trusted the LORD.

units.label: The siege ends, Zedekiah's judgment
units.note: everything warned for decades arrives at once

verses.text: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army and laid siege to the city.
And on the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, the city was breached.

Then all the officials of the king of Babylon entered and sat in the Middle Gate: Nergal-sharezer of Samgar, Nebo-sarsekim the Rabsaris, Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag, and all the rest of the officials of the king of Babylon.

When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled. They left the city at night by way of the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls, and they went out along the route to the Arabah.

But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. They seized him and brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, where he pronounced judgment on him.
There at Riblah the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and he also killed all the nobles of Judah.
Then he put out Zedekiah's eyes and bound him with bronze chains to take him to Babylon.

units.label: Jerusalem burned, the poor left in the land
units.note: the city and temple consumed by fire

verses.text: The Chaldeans set fire to the palace of the king and to the houses of the people, and they broke down the walls of Jerusalem.
Then Nebuzaradan captain of the guard carried away to Babylon the remnant of the people who had remained in the city, along with the deserters who had defected to him.
But Nebuzaradan left behind in the land of Judah some of the poor people who had no property, and at that time he gave them vineyards and fields.

units.label: Jeremiah cared for, a promise to Ebed-melech
units.note: preserved because they trusted the LORD

verses.text: Now Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had given orders about Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, saying,
“Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him; do for him whatever he says.”
So Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rabsaris, Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag, and all the captains of the king of Babylon
had Jeremiah brought from the courtyard of the guard, and they turned him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, to take him home. So Jeremiah remained among his own people.
And while Jeremiah had been confined in the courtyard of the guard, the word of the LORD had come to him:

“Go and tell Ebed-melech the Cushite that this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good, and on that day they will be fulfilled before your eyes.
But I will {{nitzal|deliver}} you on that day, declares the LORD, and you will not be delivered into the hands of the men whom you fear.
For I will surely rescue you so that you do not fall by the sword. Because you have {{batach|trusted}} in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war, declares the LORD.’”

nitzal.gloss: To deliver, rescue, or snatch away from danger. God gives this promise personally to Ebed-melech even as the whole city around him falls, showing His rescuing power reaches individuals in the very hour of national judgment.

batach.gloss: To trust, to lean on for security. The one reason given for Ebed-melech's deliverance is this trust in the LORD, not his nationality, his rank, or even his courageous act of rescuing Jeremiah, but simply that he trusted God.

basic.context: After eighteen months under siege, Jerusalem's wall is finally breached. Zedekiah flees but is captured, forced to watch his own sons executed, then blinded and bound for Babylon, exactly as Jeremiah had long warned. The city and temple are burned, its walls torn down, and most of the population deported, with only the poorest left to work the land. In the middle of this devastation, two men receive God's personal protection: Jeremiah, cared for on Nebuchadnezzar's own orders, and Ebed-melech the Cushite, promised deliverance because he trusted the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter reads as the direct fulfillment of decades of prophetic warning, confirming that Jeremiah's word, not the optimism of the false prophets, was true all along. It also refuses to let judgment be the whole story: even as the nation falls, God distinguishes between those who defied His word and the individuals, one Israelite and one foreigner, who honored it, showing that national judgment and personal deliverance can occur in the very same moment.
basic.originalLanguages: God promises to nitzal, deliver, Ebed-melech even as He fulfills His words of disaster against the whole city. The stated reason is that Ebed-melech had batach, trusted, in the LORD, the ordinary Hebrew word for leaning one's whole weight on someone for security, precisely what the nation as a whole had refused to do toward Babylon and toward God's word alike.
basic.typology: Ebed-melech's rescue amid citywide judgment, granted purely on the ground of trust, anticipates the New Testament pattern in which individual faith, not ethnic or national standing, is what distinguishes those who are saved from wrath.
basic.christ: Zedekiah's blinding and captivity is the tragic end of David's line reigning in Jerusalem, exactly as Jeremiah had warned Jehoiakim's line back in chapter 36, yet the very next chapters of the book will show God preserving a remnant and eventually promising a righteous Branch from David's line who will reign as king should have reigned, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.god: God is faithful to His warnings; every specific detail Jeremiah spoke about Zedekiah's capture and blindness comes to pass exactly as foretold. Yet in the same chapter God shows Himself personally attentive to individuals, sparing Jeremiah and promising Ebed-melech deliverance by name, proving that His justice toward a nation and His mercy toward the individual are never in conflict.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 25:1-12 gives the historical parallel account of Jerusalem's fall. Ezekiel 12:13 had already prophesied that Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon yet not see it, fulfilled exactly in his blinding. Hebrews 11:6 says without faith it is impossible to please God, the same trust credited to Ebed-melech. Romans 9:27 speaks of a remnant that will be saved even amid national judgment.
basic.oneStory: The fall of Jerusalem is the hinge of the Old Testament's darkest hour, the covenant curses finally executed in full, yet even here God preserves a remnant and singles out for deliverance those who trusted Him, previewing the pattern completed in Christ, through whom all who trust are rescued even as the world faces judgment.

context.literary:
The account of the fall of Jerusalem is told in barely a dozen verses, and it is told without comment. There is no lament in it, no 'alas,' no pause for the prophet's grief; those belong to Lamentations. The narrator reports dates, names, routes and deeds in the dry voice of a chronicle, and the restraint lands harder than outcry would. Jeremiah 52 gives a parallel report of the same events, and 2 Kings 25 a third, but only here is the account set between the siege chapters and the story of what the survivors did with their ruined land.

The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 to 7 follow the king, from the breach of the wall to the blinding at Riblah. Verses 8 to 10 widen to the city and its people: the burning, the deportation, the poor left behind. Verses 11 to 18 narrow again to two individuals, Jeremiah and Ebed-melech. The shape is a funnel, a catastrophe seen from the throne, then from the street, then from the cell where two men are quietly kept.

An image of sight runs through it. When Zedekiah sees the Babylonian officers sitting in the gate, he flees, verse 4. At Riblah his sons are slaughtered 'before his eyes,' verse 6, and then his eyes are put out, verse 7, so that the last thing he sees is the death of his heirs. Against this stands the word to Ebed-melech: the LORD's words will be fulfilled 'before your eyes,' verse 16, and he is to be delivered. One man sees his hopes die; the other sees the promise kept.

The last section steps back in time. Verse 15 says that the word to Ebed-melech came 'while Jeremiah had been confined in the courtyard of the guard,' which is earlier than the fall. It is placed here so that the story of the cistern in chapter 38 finds its answer after the catastrophe, the promise standing in the narrative where its keeping can be recognised. The promise also mirrors the oracle of doom: the LORD will fulfil His words 'for harm and not for good,' verse 16, and in the next breath, 'I will deliver you.'
context.historical:
The siege began on the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, which was January of 588 BC, Jeremiah 52:4. The wall was breached on the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh year, July of 586, verse 2 and 52:6, when famine in the city was so severe that people had no food. The siege thus lasted about eighteen months, with one brief interruption when an Egyptian relief force drew the Babylonian army away, 37:5.

The Babylonians set up their command in the Middle Gate, verse 3, which was the place where judges and officers sat, so that the conquerors literally held court where the city's own justice had been done. Their titles are Babylonian offices in Hebrew dress. 'Rabsaris' is a title for the chief eunuch and 'Rabmag' a title for another high officer, as the BSB footnotes say. A Babylonian tablet in the British Museum, published in 2007, names a Nabu-sharrussu-ukin as chief eunuch of Nebuchadnezzar, and most scholars take him to be the Nebo-sarsekim of this verse. The Nergal-sharezer who bore the title Rabmag is often identified with the man who later took the Babylonian throne as Neriglissar.

Zedekiah's escape route shows his priorities. He slips out by night through a gate between the two walls near the king's garden, which on the evidence of Nehemiah 3:15 lay in the south-east of the city near the Pool of Shelah, and then heads for the Arabah, the Jordan Valley, probably aiming for Transjordan. He is caught in the plains of Jericho and taken some three hundred kilometres north to Riblah in the land of Hamath, where Nebuchadnezzar had his headquarters. The king's sons and the nobles are put to death, and the king is blinded and bound in bronze for the journey to Babylon. Blinding was an established ancient penalty for a rebel vassal, and killing the heirs ended the dynasty's claim.

Verse 10 records an act of policy as well as mercy. The poor who had nothing were left in the land and given vineyards and fields, so that someone would work the soil and the land continue to yield. Jeremiah 52:28-30 gives modest totals for the three deportations, 3,023, 832 and 745. Excavations in Jerusalem's City of David have found a layer of burning and Babylonian-type arrowheads from this period, though the text of Jeremiah 39 itself does not name the temple, which 52:13 does.
context.canonical:
The chapter is where the long line of warnings reaches its fulfilment, and each detail can be traced to an earlier word. Jeremiah had said that Zedekiah would be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and spared no pity, 21:7, that he would not escape and would see the king of Babylon 'eye to eye,' 32:4-5, and that the city would be burned, 21:10. Ezekiel, from exile, had pictured a prince leaving by night, digging through a wall, covering his face, and being taken to Babylon but not seeing it, Ezekiel 12:12-13. The details of 39:4-7 are the answer.

Behind those prophets stands the covenant. Deuteronomy 28:36 foretold that the LORD would bring the people and 'the king you appoint' to a nation they had not known, and verse 28 spoke of blindness, and Leviticus 26:31-33 foretold the cities in rubble and the people scattered among the nations. 2 Chronicles 36:17-20 narrates the same fall as the LORD's giving them into Nebuchadnezzar's hand. Lamentations 4:19-20 gives the street-level view of the escape, with pursuers 'swifter than the eagles' and the LORD's anointed, in whose shadow they thought they would live, 'captured in their pits.'

The promise to Ebed-melech belongs to a series of rescues within judgment. Noah was found righteous in a doomed generation, Genesis 7:1; Rahab and her household were spared at Jericho because she hid the spies, Joshua 6:25; and Baruch is promised his life as a 'spoil of war' wherever he goes, Jeremiah 45:5. The preserved remnant of Isaiah 10:20-22 and the good figs of Jeremiah 24:5-7, whom the LORD keeps in view 'for good,' belong to the same line.

The New Testament takes the chapter up in two ways. Jesus warns, in words that echo the prophets, of Jerusalem surrounded by armies and the days when 'all that is written' will be fulfilled, Luke 21:20-24, urging those in Judea to flee. And Paul and Peter apply the principle of the preserved remnant: Romans 9:27 quotes Isaiah that only a remnant will be saved, and 2 Peter 2:9 says that 'the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wants his readers, the exiles, to see three things at once. First, the catastrophe was no accident of geography or of Babylonian strength. Every step of it had been announced, and Jeremiah's earlier words about Zedekiah's capture, his sons, his journey and his eyes are shown being kept to the letter. In this way the chapter answers the question the exiles were asking, who was in control, by showing that the LORD had not been overpowered; His own word had been carried out.

Second, he wants the exiles to understand where responsibility lay, and the account is careful about the details of the oath and the flight. The king who ran, who had ignored the prophet, who left his people in the night, is the one who is judged before the city is burned. The chapter keeps its attention on him, then moves to the city, as if the fall of the people followed from the failure of the one who should have led them.

Third, he means the chapter to hold out a thread of hope that does not undo the judgment. Jeremiah is kept and honoured by the conqueror, and Ebed-melech is told he will be delivered because he trusted. These two stories show that in the darkest season, God knows who belongs to Him. The author is writing for people who needed to hear that the ruin of Jerusalem did not mean the ruin of every faithful person in it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how a particular city fell at a particular moment, and it does not lay down how God must deal with every nation in every age. The horrors of verses 6 and 7, the executed sons and the blinding, are what Babylon did, and they are reported as history, not commended as justice or required as a pattern. It would be a serious mistake to read them as divine approval of every cruelty a conqueror commits. Jeremiah himself says that Babylon will be punished for its own guilt after seventy years, Jeremiah 25:12.

Likewise the generosity to the poor in verse 10 and the care for Jeremiah in verse 12 describe Nebuchadnezzar's policy, not a principle that foreign powers will always be kind. They show that God can work through a pagan ruler's decisions to keep His people.

What the passage does teach for any age is the reliability of God's word, both its warnings and its promises, and the place of trust in the way a person meets disaster. The verdict on Ebed-melech is the statement of that principle: he is rescued 'because you have trusted in Me,' verse 18. It is a promise to a particular man, but it is also a pattern that the New Testament affirms in its own terms, Romans 10:11.

debates.question: Why does the chapter pause its account of a citywide catastrophe to focus on two individuals, Jeremiah and Ebed-melech?

views.label: To vindicate the true prophet and his message
views.case: Jeremiah's preservation, care, and freedom to remain in the land directly validate everything he had preached, contrasting his fate with the officials and false prophets who opposed him.

views.label: To establish a pattern of individual deliverance within corporate judgment
views.case: Singling out Ebed-melech by name and reason, his trust, models for every later reader that national catastrophe does not erase God's attention to and rescue of individuals who trust Him, a pattern the New Testament develops fully.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge: the chapter's personal focus exists precisely to show that the same God who judges a nation also knows by name those who trust Him.

debates.question: How does Jeremiah's release in 39:11-14 fit with 40:1-6, where he is found in chains at Ramah?

views.label: Two stages of one event
views.case: In 39:14 Jeremiah is taken from the courtyard of the guard and handed to Gedaliah. Chapter 40:1 says that Nebuzaradan later found him in chains among the captives bound for Babylon at Ramah. On this reading Jeremiah was released into Gedaliah's care and then swept up by mistake in the roundup of the deportees, so Nebuzaradan freed him a second time.

views.label: Two accounts told from different angles
views.case: Chapter 39 gives a short summary of Jeremiah's fate, and chapter 40 supplies the fuller version of the same release, with the captain's speech at Ramah. The apparent difference then comes from the narrator's different purposes, and nothing needs to be harmonised.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle it. What both accounts share matters more: the Babylonian captain, acting on Nebuchadnezzar's orders, freed Jeremiah and left him free to choose where to live.

debates.question: How can Zedekiah both 'see the king of Babylon eye to eye' and 'not see' Babylon, and 'die in peace' yet die in custody?

views.label: The statements apply to different moments
views.case: Jeremiah 32:4 and 34:3 say he will meet Nebuchadnezzar face to face, which happens at Riblah, verse 5. Ezekiel 12:13 says he will be brought to Babylon but not see it, which happens because he is blinded just after. The two prophecies describe two stages in a single sequence.

views.label: 'In peace' means not by the sword
views.case: Jeremiah 34:4-5 promises that Zedekiah will not die by the sword but in peace, with spices burned for him. Jeremiah 52:11 says that he was kept in custody until the day of his death. Many readers take 'in peace' as the contrast to death in battle or by execution, and consider that the burning of spices for him is a conditional promise that his own choices set aside.

debates.bearing: The chapter shows the care with which these oracles are matched to their fulfilment, and where something remains open, it keeps the focus on the fact that Zedekiah's life ended as Jeremiah had warned if he refused to surrender.

study.originalLanguages:
The most revealing phrase is in verse 5. Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah 'pronounced judgment' on Zedekiah, which in Hebrew is literally that he 'spoke judgments with him,' a legal idiom for passing sentence. The same expression is used of God Himself earlier in the book. In Jeremiah 1:16 the LORD says, 'I will pronounce My judgments against them for all their wickedness,' and in 4:12, 'Now I also pronounce judgments against them.' What God said He would do, Nebuchadnezzar now does in the narrator's words. The conqueror becomes the instrument of a sentence that was first the LORD's.

In verse 6 the king of Babylon 'slaughtered' the sons and the nobles. The verb is shachat, the ordinary word for killing an animal for sacrifice, as in Leviticus 1:5. The narrator uses it with no ornament, and the reader hears something of the grim reversal of a city that had filled its worship with sacrifices and was now itself slaughtered.

Verse 16 says that the LORD will fulfil His words 'for harm and not for good.' The phrase picks up Jeremiah 21:10, where He had set His face against the city for the same reason, and it reverses another: in 24:6 He promised to keep His eyes on the exiles 'for good.' The Hebrew words are ra'ah and tovah, harm and good, and the whole book moves between them. In this verse they stand together, harm for the city, and in the verse after, the promise that Ebed-melech will be spared.

The final verse gives the idiom that deserves most attention. Ebed-melech is to escape with his life 'like a spoil of war.' The Hebrew shalal is the plunder of a battle. A soldier on a lost field who comes away with his life has taken it as his booty, as the one prize the day has left him. Jeremiah uses this phrase four times: 21:9, 38:2, 39:18 and 45:5, and each time it is a promise of survival where there is nothing else to be saved. Baruch, who wanted great things for himself, is told he will have his life as shalal; Ebed-melech the same. The word is both a humbling and a gift: nothing else will be rescued, but the life itself is kept.

The name of the king deserves a note. Nebuchadnezzar changed Mattaniah's name to Zedekiah, Tsidqiyyahu, which carries the sense 'the LORD is my righteousness' or 'the LORD's righteousness.' Jeremiah 23:6 promises a future king whose name will be 'The LORD Our Righteousness,' and 33:16 gives the name to Jerusalem. The reigning king bears the name of the promise and does not fulfil it, a point that Jeremiah's hearers could not have missed.

Last, the titles of the Babylonian officers carry the Akkadian word for 'chief' as rab, in Rabsaris and Rabmag. The BSB footnote explains that the first was the chief eunuch and the second probably a chief soothsayer or chief of princes. The narrator preserves the foreign titles untranslated, a sign of how alien the authorities now sitting in Jerusalem's gate are.

typology.type: The righteous kept within a doomed city, 39:15-18
typology.fulfillment: Ebed-melech is saved in the midst of a judgment that falls on everyone else. The pattern is old: Noah, found righteous in his generation, Genesis 7:1, and Rahab spared at Jericho, Joshua 6:25. Peter draws the lesson from such stories, that 'the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment,' 2 Peter 2:9. The escalation is that the final rescue is not from a siege but from the coming wrath, and the one who delivers is Jesus, 1 Thessalonians 1:10. The type falls short in that Ebed-melech's rescue is from a sword, while believers are rescued from condemnation, Romans 8:1.

typology.type: The last king of David's line, named for righteousness, 39:6-7
typology.fulfillment: Zedekiah's name means that the LORD is righteousness, and his reign ends in captured sons, put-out eyes and bronze chains. Jeremiah 23:5-6 promises another king of David's line, a righteous Branch, called 'The LORD Our Righteousness.' In Christ that name finds its occupant, for He 'has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' 1 Corinthians 1:30. The correspondence is by contrast: the king in whom the name failed and the King in whom it is true. The type falls short in that it shows only the failure; the fulfilment comes from a different source than Zedekiah's line.

typology.type: Jerusalem surrounded and its people led away, 39:1-9
typology.fulfillment: Jesus foretells the same sequence for the city of His own day: 'when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near,' and its people 'led captive into all the nations,' Luke 21:20-24. The fall of 586 is a pattern for the fall of 70, and both anticipate the final judgment. The pattern is not exact in its details and Jesus does not claim that it is. What carries across is the combination of warning and escape: 'let those who are in Judea flee,' Luke 21:21. Christians in Jerusalem did leave, according to early tradition, as Jeremiah's counsel of leaving had once urged.

typology.type: The poor given vineyards and fields, 39:10
typology.fulfillment: The ones who had nothing are given land at the moment the powerful are taken away. It is a small mercy by an enemy king and not a prophecy, but it echoes the way God's kingdom regularly reverses expectations: 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5. The echo has limits. In Jeremiah 40 the gift is soon lost when the remnant is scattered, while in Christ the inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:4.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the king it buries. Zedekiah is the last son of David to sit on the throne in Jerusalem, and his reign ends with his sons killed and his eyes put out. The line that began with the promise of 2 Samuel 7 seems to end here. Yet the same book that reports his fall promises a righteous Branch for David, 23:5, and the book of Jeremiah never lets go of David's house. The reader of the Gospels sees how: Christ is the 'Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16, and the name that Zedekiah carried and could not keep, the LORD our righteousness, is true of Him, 1 Corinthians 1:30.

It leads to Christ through the vindication of the prophetic word. Jesus speaks in the same line when He weeps over Jerusalem and says that her enemies will surround her, Luke 19:41-44. Jeremiah's long unheard warnings were finally verified in the fall of the city, and Jesus' own warning was verified in the generation that followed. In both cases the people who would not recognise 'the time of your visitation from God,' Luke 19:44, were those who had shut their ears to the word.

The promise to Ebed-melech leads to Christ through the principle it states. He is to be delivered, 'because you have trusted in Me,' verse 18, not because of his status or his people. Paul says the same of every believer: 'Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame,' Romans 10:11. The rescue from sword and city, in this chapter, points beyond itself to the deliverance Paul names, that Jesus is 'our deliverer from the coming wrath,' 1 Thessalonians 1:10. The Cushite who was saved by trust, and not by belonging, anticipates a people from every nation who are saved the same way.

There is also the way Christ takes the position of the people in the chapter. The covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 fall on Jerusalem in this chapter, with the king taken, the city burned and the people exiled. Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. He suffered outside the city gate, Hebrews 13:12, as Zedekiah was led out of it, but He went in the place of those who deserved the exile. The parallel is not a code that the narrator himself offers; it is the New Testament's own use of the covenant curses.

The care is to avoid reading Nebuchadnezzar as a figure of God or Ebed-melech as a figure of Christ. What the chapter supplies is the problem, the failed king and the fallen city, and the pattern of trust that is rescued.
study.god:
The chapter shows the God whose word comes to pass in precise detail. Jeremiah had said that Zedekiah would meet the king of Babylon face to face, 32:4, and the Babylonian king pronounces judgment on him at Riblah, verse 5. He had said that the city would be burned, 21:10, and verse 8 says it was. The exactness is deliberate. The narrator wants the reader to know that the LORD was neither surprised nor overpowered by what happened, and that the false prophets who promised peace, 37:19, had been speaking without His authority.

It shows a God who uses a pagan empire as His instrument and holds it to account at the same time. Nebuchadnezzar 'pronounces judgment' in a phrase that elsewhere belongs to God, yet the same book promises that after seventy years the LORD will punish the king of Babylon for his guilt, 25:12 and 50:17-18. God is not bound by the moral quality of the tool He uses. Neither is the tool excused by the use God makes of it. The book keeps both truths at once, and does not try to resolve them in terms that would limit either.

It shows justice that is exact and mercy that is personal. The judgment is on a nation and a king who had been warned for forty years, and it is carried out. Yet in the same chapter, God remembers the individual Cushite who spoke up for His prophet. The nation's ruin does not make the LORD lose sight of one man. The reason given is trust: the man who trusted is rescued, and the king who feared people more than God is not. Jeremiah 24:6 had put it as the LORD keeping His eyes on a people 'for good.' Here, His eyes are on one named person.

It shows a God who keeps a remnant. The poor who were left are not abandoned: the land is theirs to farm, and the prophet is among them. Isaiah 10:20-22 and Romans 9:27 make the principle general, that judgment never swallows up the whole of God's people.

For worship, the chapter calls us to take the whole counsel of God's word seriously, its threats and its promises together; to lament, as Lamentations does, over what sin costs; and to trust the God who sees each person who leans on Him, even when the walls around them are down.

crossReferences.note: The earlier oracle delivered when Zedekiah first sent to ask for a miracle: He and his officers will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and not spared. Chapter 39 is the fulfilment, with the same names, the same enemy and the same pitiless outcome.

Zedekiah is told he will not escape, that he will speak with the king of Babylon face to face and see him eye to eye, and be taken to Babylon. Riblah, in 39:5, is exactly this meeting, and the bitterness of it is that the first thing he sees is his judge.

Ezekiel, in exile, acts out the prince's flight by night through a hole in the wall, with his face covered, and says he will be brought to Babylon yet not see it. The blinding in 39:7 makes the sign literal, and it shows how two prophets in two countries spoke one word.

The parallel account names what chapter 39 leaves out. Nebuzaradan burned the house of the LORD, the royal palace and all the major buildings, and broke down the walls. Reading the two together shows how selectively the narrator of chapter 39 tells the story, keeping the spotlight on the king and then on the two individuals.

The street-level view of the same escape: pursuers swifter than eagles, and the LORD's anointed, in whose shadow they thought they would live among the nations, captured in their pits. The poem gives voice to the grief that the narrator of Jeremiah 39 leaves unspoken.

Long before, Moses had warned that the LORD would bring the people and the king they appointed to a nation they had not known. Zedekiah's journey to Babylon is the covenant curse made specific, and it shows that the sanctions of Sinai still stood.

Baruch is told he will have his life as a 'spoil of war' wherever he goes, the same idiom given to Ebed-melech in 39:18. The pairing of the scribe and the Cushite shows that this kind of promise is for those who are not seeking great things, but are trusting God.

Rahab, a foreigner who hid the spies, is spared when Jericho is destroyed and lives among Israel to this day. Ebed-melech, a Cushite who spoke up for the prophet, is spared when Jerusalem falls. In both stories, God's judgment includes a named, trusting outsider.

The LORD will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign wisely and be called 'The LORD Our Righteousness.' The name echoes Zedekiah's own, and the promise stands over the ruin of 39:6-7 as the hope that his failure could not cancel.

Jesus foretells Jerusalem surrounded by armies, its people falling by the sword and led captive into all the nations. He speaks in the voice of the prophets, and His words show that the fall of 586 was understood as the pattern for later judgments.

Peter draws the general principle from Noah and Lot that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials while holding the unrighteous for judgment. Ebed-melech is one of the Old Testament's clearest living illustrations of that sentence.

Christ has become for us our righteousness. This verse is the New Testament's reply to the name of the last king of Judah, whose title meant righteousness and who could not supply it; the righteousness that Zedekiah's name promised is found in Christ.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden and a command, and with an exile eastward when the command is broken. The long middle of the story is a series of returns and departures, and the fall of Jerusalem is the second great exile, a larger reenactment of Eden. A people given a land and a house for God's presence, who had been told that they could keep the land by keeping the covenant, lose both. The city that was supposed to be the place where God's presence met His people is razed, and the king God promised to David's house is led away blind. Everything the exiles had trusted in is taken at once.

This chapter is where the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 arrive. They were not an unspoken threat; they had been recited, taught and sworn to. The long forty-year ministry of Jeremiah had been God's patient attempt to prevent the fall, and the fall itself is not the failure of that ministry but its verification.

Yet the chapter does not end in despair. Ebed-melech's promise and Jeremiah's preservation are small signs of a larger principle that runs through the whole canon: God keeps a remnant. Noah, Rahab and the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal belong to the same line, and so do the exiles whom Jeremiah's good figs represent. The destruction of the city is not the destruction of the people of God.

The story goes on in Christ. The king whose name meant righteousness failed; the Branch for whom Jeremiah hoped is the King who is righteousness, and who reigns. Jesus warned of another siege, and He wept over the city, and then He did what no Judean king had done: He went out of the city to die for it, Hebrews 13:12, and rose. In Him the exile is finally undone, since the One who bore the curse brings those who trust Him home.

The new creation completes the reversal. The nations' kings walk into a city whose gates are never shut, and the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 21:25 and 22:2. Nothing there can be besieged, and no one flees by night through a gap in the wall. The promise given to a Cushite court official, that those who trust will be delivered, is kept at its full size for a people from every nation.

quiz.q: What happens to Zedekiah when he tries to flee the falling city?

options.text: He is captured in the plains of Jericho, forced to watch his sons killed, then blinded and bound for Babylon.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7 record this exact sequence at Riblah.

options.text: He successfully escapes to Egypt and rules from exile.
options.note: He is captured before reaching safety and never escapes to Egypt.

options.text: He surrenders peacefully and is allowed to keep his throne under Babylonian oversight.
options.note: He flees rather than surrenders, and is captured, blinded, and deposed, not allowed to keep his throne.

options.text: He is executed immediately at the city gate.
options.note: He is not executed but blinded and taken captive to Babylon; his sons and the nobles are the ones killed.

quiz.q: What happens to Jerusalem itself after the city is breached?

options.text: The palace and houses are burned, the walls broken down, and most of the people carried to Babylon.
options.note: Verses 8 to 9 describe the burning, the demolished walls, and the deportation.

options.text: The city is spared destruction in exchange for tribute.
options.note: The city and temple are burned and the walls torn down, not spared.

options.text: Only the temple is destroyed while the rest of the city remains standing.
options.note: The palace and the people's houses are also burned, and the walls are broken down.

options.text: The entire population, including the poorest, is deported with nothing left behind.
options.note: Verse 10 specifies that the poorest, who had no property, were left behind and given vineyards and fields.

quiz.q: How is Jeremiah treated after the city falls?

options.text: Nebuchadnezzar personally orders that he be cared for and not harmed, and he remains in the land with his own people.
options.note: Verses 11 to 14 record this direct order from the Babylonian king and Jeremiah's release to Gedaliah.

options.text: He is executed along with the other officials of Judah.
options.note: He is specifically spared and cared for by direct order of Nebuchadnezzar.

options.text: He is deported to Babylon along with the rest of the exiles.
options.note: He is explicitly kept in the land, not deported to Babylon.

options.text: He is left to fend for himself with no protection or provision.
options.note: He receives direct royal protection and provision, not neglect.

quiz.q: What promise does God give to Ebed-melech the Cushite, and on what basis?

options.text: That he will be delivered and not fall by the sword, because he trusted in the LORD.
options.note: Verses 17 to 18 state this promise and its stated basis, his trust in the LORD.

options.text: That he will be made a ruler over the remnant left in the land.
options.note: No promise of rulership is given; the promise is specifically deliverance and preserved life.

options.text: That his descendants will inherit the land of Judah.
options.note: The promise concerns his own personal deliverance, not a land inheritance for descendants.

options.text: That he will be exiled to Babylon but treated well there.
options.note: The promise is that he will escape with his life, not that he will be exiled, even a comfortable exile.

quiz.q: What is the theological significance of Jeremiah and Ebed-melech both being spared in this chapter?

options.text: It shows that even amid national judgment, God personally distinguishes and preserves those who honored His word and trusted Him.
options.note: Both men's fates are explicitly tied to their faithfulness or trust, set against the fate of the officials and the city as a whole.

options.text: It shows that only native born Israelites can receive God's favor.
options.note: Ebed-melech is explicitly a foreigner, a Cushite, and still receives God's promise of deliverance.

options.text: It shows that God's judgment on Jerusalem was actually a mistake being corrected.
options.note: The judgment on Jerusalem is presented as the just fulfillment of long standing warnings, not a mistake.

options.text: It shows that political rank determined who survived the siege.
options.note: Ebed-melech's rank as a court official is mentioned, but the stated reason for his deliverance is his trust in the LORD, not his rank.

questions: Everything Jeremiah warned for forty years came to pass in this one chapter, exactly as he said. Where do you need to trust that God's word will prove true in your own life, even when fulfillment is delayed?

Ebed-melech was preserved for one stated reason, that he trusted the LORD, not for his rank or nationality. Where is your own security resting right now, and is it in something God has actually promised to hold?
God cared personally for Jeremiah even in the middle of a citywide catastrophe. How does knowing God attends to individuals even amid larger disaster change how you face a hard season?
Zedekiah's reign ends exactly as warned because he never acted on the truth he privately knew. What warning has God already given you that you have not yet acted on?
The judgment on Jerusalem was real and total, yet it was not the end of God's story with His people. Where do you need hope that God's judgment on sin is never His final word for those who trust Him?

translationNotes.note: The precise dating to the ninth day of the fourth month matches 2 Kings 25:3 and Lamentations, anchoring the fall of Jerusalem to a specific, remembered date in Israel's later liturgical calendar of mourning.

Zedekiah's blinding fulfills the seemingly contradictory prophecies that he would be brought to Babylon, Jeremiah 32:5, yet would not see it, Ezekiel 12:13, since he was blinded before being taken there.

Leaving the poorest behind with vineyards and fields shows Babylonian policy aimed to keep the land productive rather than leave it entirely desolate, a detail that sets up the following narrative under Gedaliah.
